{{short description|Problem in algebraic geometry}}
In [[algebraic geometry]], the problem of '''residual intersection''' asks the following:
:''Given a subset ''Z'' in the intersection <math>\bigcap_{i=1}^r X_i</math> of varieties, understand the complement of ''Z'' in the intersection; i.e., the '''residual set''' to ''Z''.''
The intersection determines a class <math>(X_1 \cdots X_r)</math>, the [[intersection product]], in the [[Chow group]] of an ambient space and, in this situation, the problem is to understand the class, the '''residual class''' to ''Z'':
:<math>(X_1 \cdots X_r) - (X_1 \cdots X_r)^Z</math>
where <math>-^Z</math> means the part supported on ''Z''; classically the degree of the part supported on ''Z'' is called the '''equivalence''' of ''Z''.<!-- Why??? -->

The two principal applications are the solutions to problems in [[enumerative geometry]] (e.g., [[Steiner's conic problem]]) and the derivation of the [[multiple-point formula]], the formula allowing one to count or enumerate the points in a fiber even when they are [[Infinitesimal|infinitesimally close]].

The problem of residual intersection goes back to the 19th century.{{citation needed|date=March 2019}} The modern formulation of the problems and the solutions is due to Fulton and MacPherson. To be precise, they develop the [[intersection theory]] by a way of solving the problems of residual intersections (namely, by the use of the [[Segre class]] of a [[normal cone]] to an intersection). A generalization to a situation where the assumption on regular embedding is weakened is due to {{harvtxt|Kleiman|1981}}.

== Definition ==
The following definition is due to {{harv|Kleiman|1981}}.

Let
:<math>Z \subset W \subset A</math>
be closed embeddings, where ''A'' is an [[algebraic variety]] and ''Z'', ''W'' are closed subschemes. Then, by definition, the '''residual scheme''' to ''Z'' is
:<math>R(Z, W) = \mathbf{P}(I(Z, W)^*)</math>.
where <math>\mathbf{P}</math> is the [[projectivization]] (in the classical sense) and <math>\mathcal{I}(Z, W) \subset \mathcal{O}_W</math> is the [[ideal sheaf]] defining <math>Z \hookrightarrow W</math>.

Note: if <math>B(Z, W)</math> is the blow-up of <math>W</math> along <math>Z</math>, then, for <math>\mathcal{I} = \mathcal{I}(Z, W)</math>, the surjection <math display="inline">\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal{I}) \to \bigoplus_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathcal{I}^n</math> gives the closed embedding:
:<math>B(Z, W) \hookrightarrow R(Z, W)</math>,
which is the isomorphism if the inclusion <math>Z \hookrightarrow W</math> is a regular embedding.

{{math_theorem|name=Residual intersection formula|math_statement=Let <math>N_i = N_{X_i} Y|_Z </math>.

:<math>(X_1 \cdots X_r \cdot V)_Z = c(N_1) \cdots c(N_r) s(C_Z V)</math>

where ''s''(''C''<sub>''Z''</sub> ''X'') denotes the [[Segre class]] of the normal cone to ''Z'' in ''X'' and the subscript ''Z'' signifies the part supported on ''Z''.}}

If the <math>Z_i</math> are scheme-theoretic connected components of <math>\bigcap_i X_i</math>, then
:<math>(X_1 \cdots X_r) = \sum_i (X_1 \cdots X_r)^{Z_i}</math>

For example, if ''Y'' is the [[projective space]], then [[Bézout's theorem]] says the degree of <math>\bigcap_i X_i</math> is <math>\prod_i \deg(X_i)</math> and so the above is a different way to count the contributions to the degree of the intersection. In fact, in applications, one combines Bézout's theorem.

Let <math>X_i \hookrightarrow Y</math> be [[regular embedding]]s of schemes, separated and of finite type over the base field; for example, this is the case if ''X''<sub>''i''</sub> are effective Cartier divisors (e.g., hypersurfaces). The [[intersection product]] of <math>X_i</math>
:<math>(X_1 \cdots X_r)</math>
is an element of the Chow group of ''Y'' and it  can be written as
:<math>(X_1 \cdots X_r) = \sum_i m_i \alpha_i</math>
where <math>m_i</math> are positive integers.

Given a set ''S'', we let
:<math>(X_1 \cdots X_r)^S = \sum_{\operatorname{Supp}(\alpha_i) \subset S} m_i \alpha_i.</math>

== Formulae ==
===Quillen's excess-intersection formula ===
The formula in the topological setting is due to {{harvtxt|Quillen|1971}}.

Now, suppose we are given ''Y{{''}}'' → ''Y''{{'}} and suppose ''i{{'}}'': ''X''{{'}} = ''X'' ×<sub>''Y''</sub> ''Y''{{'}} → ''Y''{{'}} is regular of codimension ''d{{'}}'' so that one can define ''i{{'}}''<sup>!</sup> as before. Let ''F'' be the excess bundle of ''i'' and ''i<sup>'</sup>''; that is, it is the pullback to ''X{{''}}'' of the quotient of ''N'' by the normal bundle of ''i{{'}}''. Let ''e''(''F'') be the [[Euler class]] (top [[Chern class]]) of ''F'', which we view as a homomorphism from ''A''<sub>''k''−''d{{'}}''</sub>&nbsp;(''X{{''}}'') to ''A''<sub>''k''−''d''</sub>(''X{{''}}''). Then

{{math_theorem|name=Excess intersection formula|math_statement=<math>i^! = e(F) {i'}^!</math>}}
where ''i''<sup>!</sup> is determined by the morphism ''Y{{''}}'' → ''Y{{'}}'' → ''Y''.<!-- I don't like this abuse of notation but this is what Fulton does. -->

Finally, it is possible to generalize the above construction and formula to [[complete intersection morphism]]s; this extension is discussed in § 6.6. as well as Ch. 17 of loc. cit.<!-- not sure the best way to discuss orientation.In algebraic topology, a choice of an orientation of a real vector bundle gives rise to a [[Gysin homomorphism]]. One can do an analog of this for (global) [[complete intersection morphism]]s. Let ''f'': ''X'' → ''Y'' be a complete intersection morphism; by definition, it factors as a regular embedding ''i'':  ''X'' → ''Z'' followed by a [[smooth morphism]] ''p''.-->

''Proof'': One can deduce the intersection formula from the rather explicit form of a Gysin homomorphism. Let ''E'' be a vector bundle on ''X'' of rank ''r'' and {{nowrap|''q'': '''P'''(''E'' ⊕ 1) → ''X''}} the [[projective bundle]] (here 1 means the trivial line bundle). As usual, we identity '''P'''(''E'' ⊕ 1) as a disjoint union of '''P'''(''E'') and ''E''. Then there is the tautological exact sequence
:<math>0 \to \mathcal{O}(-1) \to q^*E \oplus 1 \to \xi \to 0</math>
on '''P'''(''E'' ⊕ 1). We claim the Gysin homomorphism is given as
:<math>A_k(E) \to A_{k-r}(X), \, x \mapsto q_*(e(\xi) \overline{x})</math>
where ''e''(''ξ'') = ''c''<sub>''r''</sub>(''ξ'') is the Euler class of ξ and <math>\overline{x}</math> is an element of {{nowrap|''A''<sub>''k''</sub>('''P'''(''E'' ⊕ 1))}} that restricts to ''x''.<!-- one should be able to guess this formula from topology? --> Since the injection {{nowrap|''q''<sup>*</sup>: ''A''<sub>''k''−''r''</sub>(''X'') → ''A''<sub>''k''</sub>('''P'''(''E'' ⊕ 1))}} splits, we can write
:<math>\overline{x} = q^* y + z</math>
where ''z'' is a class of a cycle supported on '''P'''(''E'').
By the Whitney sum formula, we have: ''c''(''q''<sup>*</sup>''E'') = (1&nbsp;−&nbsp;''c''<sub>1</sub>(''O''(1)))''c''(''ξ'') and so
:<math>e(\xi) = \sum_0^r c_1(\mathcal{O}(1))^i c_{r-i}(q^* E).</math>
Then we get:
:<math>q_*(e(\xi) q^* y) = \sum_{i=0}^r s_{i-r}(E \oplus 1) c_{r-i}(E) y</math>
where ''s''<sub>''I''</sub>(''E'' ⊕ 1) is the ''i''-th [[Segre class]]. Since the zeroth term of a Segre class is the identity and its negative terms are zero, the above expression equals ''y''. Next, since the restriction of ξ to '''P'''(''E'') has a nowhere-vanishing section and ''z'' is a class of a cycle supported on '''P'''(''E''), it follows that {{nowrap|''e''(ξ)''z'' <nowiki>=</nowiki> 0}}. Hence, writing π for the projection map of ''E'' and ''j'' for the inclusion ''E'' to '''P'''(''E''⊕1), we get:
:<math>\pi^* q_*(e(\xi) \overline{x}) = \pi^*(y) = j^* q^* y = j^*(\overline{x} - z) = j^*(\overline{x}) = x</math>
where the second-to-last equality is because of the support reason as before. This completes the proof of the explicit form of the Gysin homomorphism.

The rest is formal and straightforward. We use the exact sequence
:<math>0 \to \xi' \to \xi \to r^* F \to 0</math>
where ''r'' is the projection map for . Writing ''P'' for the closure of the specialization of ''V'', by the Whitney sum formula and the projection formula, we have:
:<math>i^!(V) = r_*(e(\xi) P) = r_*(e(r^*F) e(\xi') P) = e(F) r_*(e(\xi') P) = e(F) {i'}^!(V).</math>
<math>\square</math>

One special case of the formula is the [[self-intersection formula]], which says: given a regular embedding ''i'': ''X'' → ''Y'' with normal bundle ''N'',
:<math>i^*i_* = e(N).</math>
(To get this, take ''Y{{'}}'' = ''Y{{''}}'' = ''X''.) For example, from this and the [[projection formula]], when ''X'', ''Y'' are smooth, one can deduce the formula:
:<math>i_*(x) i_*(y) = i_*(e(N) xy).</math>
in the Chow ring of ''Y''.

Let <math>f: \widetilde{Y} \to Y</math> be the blow-up along a closed subscheme ''X'', <math>\widetilde{X}</math> the exceptional divisor and <math>g: \widetilde{g}: \widetilde{X} \to X</math> the restriction of ''f''. Assume ''f'' can be written as a [[closed immersion]] followed by a [[smooth morphism]] (for example, ''Y'' is quasi-projective). Then, from <math>f^* i_* = i^! g^*</math>, one gets:

{{math_theorem|name=Jouanolou's key formula|math_statement=<math>f^* i_* = {i'}_* e(F) g^*</math>.}}

== Examples ==
Throughout the example section, the base field is algebraically closed and has characteristic zero. All the examples below (except the first one) are from {{harvtxt|Fulton|1998}}.

=== Example: intersection of two plane curves containing the same component ===
Let <math>C_1 = Z(x_0x_1)</math> and <math>C_2 = Z(x_0x_2)</math> be two plane curves in <math>\mathbb{P}^2</math>. Set theoretically, their intersection<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
C_1 \cap C_2 &= Z(x_1,x_2) \cup Z(x_0) \\
&= [1:0:0] \cup \{[0:a:b] \in \mathbb{P}^2 \} \\
&= Z_1\cup Z_2
\end{align}</math></blockquote>is the union of a point and an embedded <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math>. By [[Bézout's theorem]], it is expected this intersection should contain <math>4</math> points since it is the intersection of two conics, so interpreting this intersection requires a residual intersection. Then<blockquote><math>(C_1\cap C_2)^{Z_1} = \left\{ \frac{
    c(N_{C_1/\mathbb{P}^2}) c(N_{C_2/\mathbb{P}^2})
}{
    c(N_{Z_1/\mathbb{P}^2})
} \right\}_{0} \in A_{0}(Z_1)</math>

<math>(C_1\cap C_2)^{Z_2} = \left\{ \frac{
    c(N_{C_1/\mathbb{P}^2}) c(N_{C_2/\mathbb{P}^2})
}{
    c(N_{Z_2/\mathbb{P}^2})
} \right\}_{1} \in A_{1}(Z_2)</math></blockquote>Since <math>C_1,C_2</math> are both degree <math>2</math> hypersurfaces, their normal bundle is the pullback of <math>\mathcal{O}(2)</math>, hence the numerator of the two residual components is<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
c(\mathcal{O}(2))c(\mathcal{O}(2)) &= (1 + 2[H])(1 + 2[H]) \\
&= 1 + 4[H] + 4[H]^2
\end{align}</math></blockquote>Because <math>Z_1</math> is given by the vanishing locus <math>Z(x_1,x_2)</math> its normal bundle is <math>\mathcal{O}(1)\oplus \mathcal{O}(1)</math>, hence<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
c(N_{Z_1/\mathbb{P}^2}) &= c(\mathcal{O}(1)\oplus \mathcal{O}(1)) \\
&= (1 + [H])(1 + [H]) \\
&= 1 + 2[H] + [H]^2 \\
&= 1
\end{align}</math></blockquote>since <math>Z_1</math> is dimension <math>0</math>. Similarly, the numerator is also <math>1</math>, hence the residual intersection is of degree <math>1</math>, as expected since <math>Z_1</math> is the complete intersection given by the vanishing locus <math>Z(x_1,x_2)</math>. Also, the normal bundle of <math>Z_2</math> is <math>\mathcal{O}(1)</math> since it is given by the vanishing locus <math>Z(x_0)</math>, so<blockquote><math>c(N_{Z_2}/X) = 1 + [H]</math></blockquote>Inverting <math>c(N_{Z_2}/X)</math> gives the series<blockquote><math>\frac{1}{1 + [H]} = 1 - [H] + [H]^2</math></blockquote>hence <blockquote><math>\begin{align}
\frac{c(N_{C_1/\mathbb{P}^2}) c(N_{C_2/\mathbb{P}^2})}{c(N_{Z_2/\mathbb{P}^2})} 
=& (1 + 4[H] + 4[H]^2)(1 - [H] + [H]^2) \\
=& (1 - [H] + [H]^2) + (4[H] - 4[H]^2) + 4[H]^2 \\
=&1 +3[H] + [H]^2 \\
=&1 + 3[H]

\end{align}</math></blockquote>giving the residual intersection of <math>3[H]</math> for <math>Z_2</math>. Pushing forward these two classes gives <math>4[H]^2</math> in <math>A^*(\mathbb{P}^2)</math>, as desired.

=== Example: the degree of a curve in three surfaces ===
Let <math>X_1, X_2, X_3 \subset \mathbb{P}^3</math> be three surfaces. Suppose the scheme-theoretic intersection <math>\bigcap X_i</math> is the disjoint union of a smooth curve ''C'' and a zero-dimensional schem ''S''. One can ask: what is the degree of ''S''? This can be answered by [[#formula]].

=== Example: conics tangent to given five lines ===
The plane conics are parametrized by <math>\mathbb{P}^{\binom{2+2}{2}-1} = \mathbb{P}^5</math>. Given five general lines <math>\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_5 \subset \mathbb{P}^2</math>, let <math>H_{\ell_i} \subset \mathbb{P}^5</math> be the hypersurfaces of conics tangent to <math>\ell_i</math>; it can be shown that these hypersurfaces have degree two.<!-- we need to discuss stuff like this elsewhere in Wikipedia. -->

The [[scheme-theoretic intersection|intersection]] <math>\bigcap_i H_{\ell_i}</math> contains the [[Veronese surface]] <math>Z \simeq \mathbb{P}^2</math> consisting of double lines; it is a scheme-theoretic connected component of <math>\bigcap_i H_{\ell_i}</math>. Let <math>h = c_1(\mathcal{O}_Z(1))</math>
be the hyperplane class = the [[first Chern class]] of ''O''(1) in the [[Chow ring]] of ''Z''. Now, <math>Z = \mathbb{P}^2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^5</math> such that <math>\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^5}(1)</math> pulls-back to <math>\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^2}(2)</math> and so the [[normal cone|normal bundle]] to <math>H_{\ell_i}</math> restricted to ''Z'' is
:<math>N_{H_{\ell_i}/\mathbb{P}^5}|_Z = \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^5}(H_{\ell_i})|_Z = \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^5}(2)|_Z = \mathcal{O}_Z(4).</math>
So, the total [[Chern class]] of it is
:<math>c(N_{H_{\ell_i}/\mathbb{P}^5}|_Z) = 1+4h.</math>
Similarly, using that the normal bundle to a regular <math>X \hookrightarrow Y</math> is <math>T_Y|_X /T_X</math> as well as the [[Euler sequence]], we get that the total Chern class of the normal bundle to <math>Z \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^5</math> is
:<math>c(N_{Z/\mathbb{P}^5}) = c(T_{\mathbb{P}^5}|_Z)/c(T_Z) = c(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^5}(1)^{\oplus 6}|_Z)/c(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^2}(1)^{\oplus 3}) = (1+2h)^6/(1+ h)^3.</math>
Thus, the [[Segre class]] of <math>Z \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^5</math> is
:<math>s(Z, \mathbb{P}^5) = c(N_{Z/\mathbb{P}^5})^{-1} = 1-9h+51h^2.</math>
Hence, the equivalence of ''Z'' is
:<math>\deg((1+4h)^5(1-9h+51h^2))= 160 - 180 + 51 = 31.</math>
By [[Bézout's theorem]], the degree of <math>\bigcap_i H_{\ell_i}</math> is <math>2^5 = 32</math> and hence the residual set consists of a single point corresponding to a unique conic tangent to the given all five lines.

Alternatively, the equivalence of ''Z'' can be computed by [[#formula?]]; since <math>\deg(c_1(T_{\mathbb{P}^2})) = \deg(c_2(T_{\mathbb{P}^2})) = 3</math> and <math>\deg(Z) = 4</math>, it is:
:<math>3 + 4(3) + (40 - 10(6) + 21) \deg(Z) = 31.</math>

=== Example: conics tangent to given five conics ===
{{expand section|date=March 2019}}
{{see also|Steiner's conic problem}}

Suppose we are given five plane conics <math>C_1, \ldots, C_5 \subset \mathbb{P}^2</math> in general positions. One can proceed exactly as in the previous example. Thus, let <math>H_{C_i} \subset \mathbb{P}^5</math> be the hypersurface of conics tangent to <math>C_i</math>; it can be shown that it has degree&nbsp;6. The intersection <math>\bigcap_i H_{C_i}</math> contains the Veronese surface ''Z'' of double lines.
